stories.headline: MLB 2026 playoffs: Ranking home-field advantage for every team
stories.summary: From atmosphere to unique structures, some places are harder to play than others. Here are the clubs who benefit the most.
stories.body:
Tony Gwynn Jr. grew up going to games at Jack Murphy Stadium when his father, Tony Gwynn, played for the San Diego Padres, and he played in Petco Park himself during his own eight-year MLB career, so he has seen the dramatic evolution of the ballpark atmosphere in San Diego.

"What flies under the radar is that with the departure of the [NFL's] Chargers, this opened space for more fanatic Padres fans," Gwynn Jr. wrote in a text to ESPN. "This generation of Padre fans seems to be more fanatical than the generation I came up watching, when the fans could kind of take it or leave it. With the Padres being the only team in town now, it's just a different type of fan than it was before."

That the experience at a Padres games for fans and players -- on both teams -- has changed is indisputable. What is debatable is where Petco Park ranks in terms of home-field advantage among the eight teams still alive in the division series and battling for a World Series title.

We spoke to a number of managers and coaches -- who, of course, have all competed in the ballparks still in play -- on home-field advantage among the remaining clubs to create this ranking, based on their years of experience and feedback.

1. Yankee Stadium, New York Yankees

When the Yankees moved from their old home to the new Yankee Stadium in 2009, the initial narrative was that the new place didn't have the soul of the old place, because the new Yankee Stadium seemed bigger and more cavernous, with less intensity. But most of those we polled contend that the current Yankee Stadium provides the best home-field advantage in these playoffs.

"The combination of the crowd, the atmosphere, all of the postseason history," one NL staffer said.

"It's still the gold standard for a home field," an AL staffer said. "The fans are there early. They are loud. Their passion can be felt from Pitch 1. The event feels different. It still has the edge that impacts the opponent."

The atmosphere at Yankee Stadium has affected opposing teams in the past. During the 2017 playoffs, the Houston Astros were swept in the middle three games they played in New York of their best-of-seven ALCS. After Game 5, Houston's Carlos Beltran called a meeting, believing that his teammates were being impacted by Yankee Stadium's atmosphere, and told them they needed to calm down.

2. Petco Park, San Diego Padres

One AL staffer wrote in a text, "Petco is most improved and arguably 1-B to Yankee Stadium. The music, the vibe, the volume all impact the visiting team. The in-game is noticeably on point. The fans are all-in. It is no longer a chill place."

Nope, it is not. Due to the Western Metal Building in left field that looms over the field and the low outfield fencing, fans seem to be right on top of the players, making the whole place play like a small ballpark. But it's not small. With the expanded Gallagher Square seating, it can hold 47,000-plus fans, team president Erik Greupner said. San Diego was second in home attendance this past regular season, with 3.35 million, ranking behind only ... our next team.

3. Dodger Stadium, Los Angeles Dodgers

The Dodgers' players themselves make this a difficult place for visitors, of course, with the collection of future Hall of Famers comprising the lineup and the accomplished starting pitchers. But what was cited the most by rival staffers was the noise.

"Loud," one of the staffers said. "The speakers are incredible. The fan base is amazing."

"It's just so loud there," another said. "It's like the bass from the speakers thumps you in the chest."

4. Tropicana Field, Tampa Bay Rays

A long list of factors was cited by those polled as they addressed the difficulty for teams visiting St. Petersburg, from the inherent distraction of the nearby beaches to the way that the fan noise ricochets in the park. Most often mentioned, however, was the artificial surface and the enormous outfield, and how the Rays' team is custom built for its park, with speed (Chandler Simpson) and a pitching staff that fills the strike zone to take advantage of the spacious dimensions.

"The fast surface always matches their offensive style," one AL staffer said. "The goal has always been to not get swept there."

5. Truist Park, Atlanta Braves
Some of the staffers polled mentioned the enthusiasm of Braves fans, as well as their collective volume. A couple of them mentioned how hot it can get -- which has been the case already. When the forecast for Game 1 of the NLDS called for triple-digit temperatures, Atlanta manager Walt Weiss dismissed the impact, saying his team was accustomed to playing in that kind of weather.

6. American Family Field, Milwaukee Brewers
Brewers fans show up early and stay late, and when Jackson Chourio smashed the walk-off single to beat Padres closer Mason Miller and secure the Game 2 win, those fans shared in the sort of moment that will be remembered beyond this generation. The place was bonkers.

But the managers and coaches who responded in this poll are accustomed to noisy fans. What they find most difficult about playing in Milwaukee are the late-afternoon shadows and the working conditions. One staffer said that the clubhouse, food and batting cage are all the worst in the league, "so that makes it tougher to play there."

7. Progressive Field, Cleveland Guardians

"It's not an intimidating place for us," one staffer said. "Maybe that's because they typically have a lot of young players. They have good teams, but there's nothing that makes it a tough place to play. Not compared to some of the other places, certainly."

8. Rate Field, Chicago White Sox
"It's a neutral for me," one NL staffer said. "Nothing really stands out."

The growing popularity of the pope hats -- and the improvement of the White Sox, from setting the modern MLB single-season loss record in 2024 with 121 losses to making the playoffs and winning their first series since 2005 -- might start to change that.

stories.headline: Which Premier League players got injured in the international break?
stories.summary: All the latest news and updates on Premier League stars injuries during the first international break of the 2026-2027 club season
stories.body:
Premier League teams will be watching and hoping their star players remain healthy throughout the international break.

However, some have already sustained injuries while playing for their countries. Premier League matches resume on Oct. 10.

ESPN will be tracking the latest injuries and updates for your club's players:

Kai Havertz (Arsenal)

Arsenal's Kai Havertz was forced off in the 30th minute of the game between Netherlands and Germany on September 24th with what was described as a muscle injury.

"Both are currently undergoing an MRI," Jurgen Klopp said on RTL about Havertz and Jamal Musiala. "I hope we get the diagnosis [on Thursday] evening. But of course, this isn't great. I hope it's nothing serious. The lads are probably out for us. But hopefully, they'll be back in action relatively quickly."

On September 25 the German Football Association confirmed the attacker would be leaving Klopp's camp and return to Arsenal after suffering what they describe as a 'muscle strain.'

Brian Brobbey (Sunderland)

The powerful Sunderland attacker was also injured in the same game after picking up what looked like a hamstring injury while running for the ball. He immediately went down and signalled to the sideline.

He left the field of his own accord but did have a heavy limp as he walked down the tunnel.

Netherlands boss Xavi Hernandez said after the game: "Brian is indeed injured."

Brobbey was replaced by Joshua Zirkzee in the Dutch squad.

Zion Suzuki (Aston Villa)

The goalkeeper linked up with the Japan squad but according to reports missed the main group training session on September 22nd, according to local reports. Instead he was put on an individual session for a rib injury.

Suzuki was subsequently left out of Japan's matchday squad entirely for Thursday's 3-1 victory over Uruguay.

Dan Ballard (Sunderland)

The Sunderland defender suffered a reported hamstring injury during Northern Ireland's 1-0 victory over Georgia in the UEFA Nations League.

With the score still 0-0 as the match moved into stoppage time, Ballard chased back as Georgia counter-attacked and pulled up clutching the back of his thigh, unable to finish the match in Tbilisi.

Speaking immediately after Friday's match, manager Michael O'Neill said it was too soon to know the extent of his latest injury but will definitely miss the next three Northern Ireland games.

"We'll scan him tomorrow (Saturday), but he's certainly not going to be available for the next three games."

Alexander Isak (Liverpool)

Alexander Isak is returning to Liverpool after sustaining a "minor injury" on international duty.

The striker scored and played the full 90 minutes in Sweden's 2-1 victory over Romania in the Nations League on Friday.

But Isak, who has made a strong start to the season for Liverpool, will not feature in matches against Poland, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Romania over the remainder of the extended international break.

Bruno Fernandes (Manchester United)

The Manchester United midfielder was left out of Portugal's squad for Sunday's game against Norway.

"He played with an injury he brought from Manchester United," Portugal boss Jorge Jesus said. "He really wanted to play against Wales."

Patrick Dorgu (Manchester United)

The news for Manchester United fans who saw Fernandes absent worsened on Sunday when Dorgu was injured.

The left wing-back limped out of Denmark's match against Wales after 30 minutes.

Denmark head coach Brian Riemer told broadcaster TV2 after the game: "He has an injury and has to go home."

Cody Gakpo (Liverpool)

Liverpool forward Gakpo lasted only 17 minutes of the Netherlands' match against Serbia on Sunday. It means Liverpool are sweating over the fitness of Isak and Gakpo.

He looked in pain as he held the lower part of his right leg.

"It's his ankle, that's all I know," Netherlands boss Xavi Hernández said. "Tomorrow we will know, but hopefully it's not too important."

Noussair Mazraoui (Manchester United)

The United full-back was forced out of Morocco's Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Lesotho after 69 minutes. He was holding his back while on the floor after a challenge.

Nico O'Reilly (Manchester City)

O'Reilly missed England's win against Czechia on Tuesday night after also missing training on Monday. Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha was called into the matchday squad. O'Reilly returned to Manchester for further treatment before England played Croatia.

Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham Hotspur)

The Tottenham defender Jan Paul van Hecke picked up a foot injury in the Netherlands' clash with Serbia and withdrew from the Netherlands' squad during a training session.

No replacement will be called up for van Hecke. He is now returning to Spurs.

Christos Tzolis (Arsenal)

The Greece winger limped out of his side's draw against the Netherlands after just 18 minutes.

Tzolis pulled his shirt over his head and looked upset as he left the match early.

He represents another headache for Arsenal after Kai Havertz's prior injury for Germany.

Erling Haaland (Manchester City)

Man City's talismanic striker limped out of Norway's match against Portugal on Sunday.

Haaland gestured to the bench and requested to be substituted. He was replaced after 67 minutes.

There was no update on his fitness after Norway's defeat.

Micky van de Ven, Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham)

Van de Ven went off injured in the Netherlands' game against Serbia on Sunday.

The Tottenham defender seemingly hurt his arm in a clash with Luka Jovic.

Fellow Tottenham and Netherlands defender Van Hecke withdraw from the international squad before the Serbia game with a foot injury.

Alex Scott (Bournemouth)

Scott made his full international debut for England in a 7-0 win over Croatia but went off after 70 minutes. He has since pulled out of the squad to play Czechia and is expected to miss several weeks of action due to a thigh injury.

Ezri Konsa (Arsenal)

Konsa started for England in their 7-0 win against Croatia but withdrew from the squad to play Czechia with an injury.

International breaks this season

1. Sept. 21-Oct. 6 (between Premier League gameweeks 5 and 6)

2. Nov. 9-Nov. 17 (between Premier League gameweeks 10 and 11)

3. March 22-March 30 (between Premier League gameweeks 30 and 31)

stories.headline: Behind the scenes inside LeBron's first 76ers training camp
stories.summary: From on-court schemes to a private team dinner to an attempt at divine intervention, here's what happened in LeBron's first camp with the 76ers.
stories.body:
There might not be a more intriguing new-look team in the NBA this season than the Philadelphia 76ers.

It's not just the infusion of talent, but the rarity of the circumstances to acquire it that makes the Sixers so fascinating.

In any other year, signing forward Dean Wade to a four-year, $39 million contract and guard Anfernee Simons to a two-year, $12.3 million deal could be seen as a successful summer for a team coming off a second-round playoff appearance.

But then to trade for five-time All-Star Jaylen Brown two years after he led the Boston Celtics to the championship, making him just one of seven players in league history to change teams within two years of being named Finals MVP, made it an extraordinary offseason.

And adding LeBron James on a veteran's minimum contract made it potentially transformational.

With the Sixers playing their first preseason game Monday against the defending-champion New York Knicks, here are five key moments that have shaped their first week in training camp.

Monday, Sept. 28: four on the floor ... and a fifth in the group chat
Hours before media day opened with players posing for portraits and answering questions from local media members, the Sixers' four stars gathered on the practice floor.

They changed into their full uniforms later to be ready for photos. Their first order of business was a workout, not only to talk about, but demonstrate, how they can help one another.

All four had varying experience playing together, with Brown recently joining James and Tyrese Maxey for a few of their customary summer workouts in Los Angeles, and James playing with Joel Embiid on Team USA in 2024. But these first actions on the floor were tangible examples of the sacrifices this group has said it is willing to make for this season to be a success.

"Worked on getting to know each other," one team source told ESPN. "Camaraderie, rhythm, cadence and playing with each other."

With 36 All-Star appearances among them, each player has a game that commands extra attention from opposing defenses.

Philadelphia intends to exploit that by having its foursome work on two-man plays for when defenses inevitably overcommit.

"All four of those guys are going to be trapped somehow during the game, whether it's in the post or on the wing," the source continued. "We worked a lot on passing out of the post, making the extra pass to the corner."

Second-year guard VJ Edgecombe, the fifth starter on the team, was not part of these exercises, but there have been early indicators that he'll be included, too.

Edgecombe took it upon himself to start a group chat this summer for James and his new Sixers teammates.

"Before 'Bron got [here], I was like, 'Yo, I'm making a group chat: Me, 'Rese, JB, Joel,'" Edgecombe said of his initial plan he shared with Maxey. "And then 'Bron came, and obviously I don't got LeBron James' number, so ... I told Tyrese to do it. I asked Tyrese if he could [add him]. ... But it was my idea. Anyone telling you it was their idea, they're lying."

The 21-year-old's gesture seems to have gone over just fine with the vet nearly twice his age.

When ESPN asked James on media day for his first thought when hearing Edgecombe's name, he replied:

"A star."

Tuesday, Sept. 29: "The Vision" is shared
As eager to take the floor as everyone was Tuesday morning at the team practice facility in Camden, N.J., Sixers coach Nick Nurse first had something in store for his players.

Nurse, who guided the Toronto Raptors to the championship in 2019, led a 30-minute team meeting in a conference room a level above the court to address the lofty expectations this season.

"The theme of it was to try to set the mission and vision of the team for the year," Nurse told ESPN. "That's easy to do, but then you got to have the plan right underneath that."

Inside the room, Nurse stood in front of the team. He introduced the "pillars" he expects his team to adhere to and then detailed the plans on offense and defense and what steps the players will take to execute them. He preached holding one another accountable, sources said, and that the Sixers intend to feast in transition.

"I think a lot of the points of it were so you're not wondering why we're doing this when we're downstairs," Nurse told ESPN. ".. I'm trying to give them a little bit of a head start."

Simons, another newcomer, said the meeting was helpful.

"Just setting the tone of what we expect as a team," he said. "Just pointing out the expectations for us as a unit, what it's going to take for us to reach those expectations. It was a good meeting. Obviously, it gave us a little bit of motivation to go out there."

For James, though, this discussion was a bit of a rehash.

Nurse was on the golf course in mid-July, two weeks before James signed with the Sixers, when Nurse received a text from Klutch Sports CEO Rich Paul, asking him if he was available to talk.

After the coach confirmed that he was, Paul called and passed the phone to James.

Nurse paused his round and took a seat in his golf cart, as the two outlined an impromptu vision.

"I think the first things were just offense and defense -- the nuts and bolts of basketball," Nurse told ESPN. "He played us a couple times [since Nurse became Philadelphia's coach in 2023] and I'm saying, 'Hey, we did this because of this and this because that,' and he goes, 'Yeah, yeah, yeah, that makes sense.'

"He would kind of remember why we were doing what we were doing on offense. So that was the main thing.

"And then it kind of veered off to, 'Where's the fit? How do you see the fit?' And I was all for it. I thought there was a perfect fit for him to slot right in there and give us a lot of what we need."

Wednesday, Sept. 30: "We ain't there yet"
The collective mood of Philadelphians is often tied to the fate of the city's professional sports teams.

While the 76ers were opening training camp, the Philadelphia Phillies were closing out their season in a devastating fashion that is all-too familiar for Philly fans.

Sixers president of basketball operations Mike Gansey has enjoyed as successful a start to a tenure as any Philly sports executive thanks to the way he has built his team since being hired in May. He showed solidarity with the Phillies last week by showing up to practice in a red, fitted Phillies hat.

But even Gansey's support couldn't help the Phillies from blowing a late-inning lead in Game 1 of the playoffs for the third straight postseason, setting up an eventual 2-1 National League wild-card loss to the Atlanta Braves in their best-of-three series.

For a group attempting to end the Sixers' 43-year championship drought, in a town used to hard-luck results, divine intervention certainly couldn't hurt.

Nurse invited pastor Philip Anthony Mitchell from 2819 Church in Atlanta to address the team Wednesday.

"He was great," Gansey said. "Talked to our team for about 20 minutes ... and the guys were really locked in."

Mitchell announced the speaking engagement on his Facebook page.

"More than professional athletes with contracts, they are men with souls and real-life challenges," he wrote. "Appreciate your prayers for them and for me."

Later that evening, sources told ESPN, the team met for dinner at Lark in the suburb of Bala Cynwyd, Pennsylvania, overlooking the Schuylkill River.

The Mediterranean-style menu is cultivated by former "Top Chef" winner Nicholas Elmi. The occasion was not just another bonding experience, but it provided inspiration for Sixers rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. regarding the relationship he could eventually develop with an all-time great such as James.

"Did you see him and KCP's handshake when we were at dinner last night?" Philon asked during a live stream Thursday, referring to James greeting his former Los Angeles Lakers teammate Kentavious Caldwell-Pope at the team event. "

I was like, 'Damn, that s--- hard.' ... We ain't there yet."

Friday, Oct. 2: the farthest away but still the first
James' daily routine begins at the Sixers' training complex around 7:45 a.m., when he is met by his longtime athletic trainer, Mike Mancias, to work on his body.

There is stretching, activation and modalities to check off as he embarks on an unprecedented 24th NBA season, breaking his NBA record for player longevity with every game he plays.

And there is special attention paid to his left foot, which has chronic arthritis, sources told ESPN, and his lower back, which caused him to miss the first month of last season because of sciatica.

Practice was scheduled for 11 a.m. during the first week of training camp.

Edgecombe recalls the first time he saw James in the locker room before practice.

"He was in there before everybody," Edgecombe said. "As usual."

This, of course, despite living nearly 100 miles away in New York City.

James takes a 40-minute helicopter ride to work, with the chopper landing on the helicopter pad on top of the Sixers' business offices next to the practice facility.

The commute has invited outside curiosity but does not appear to faze anyone in the organization who are used to Sixers managing partner and primary owner Josh Harris coming and going the same way.

After Friday's practice, James' helicopter was heard inside the facility as Sixers third-year forward Justin Edwards wrapped up his media availability with reporters.

Edwards finished his final answer, turned his head toward the ceiling and joked, "Is he coming back?"

Saturday, Oct. 3: "a great first step" and a Marvel
To try to quantify the impact this revamped Sixers squad is already making on the region, consider that last fall, the team's annual Blue-White intrasquad scrimmage was held at Chase Fieldhouse in Wilmington, Delaware -- home of the G League affiliate, the Delaware Blue Coats.

Saturday's was held at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

"We're getting people that want to come ... to a scrimmage. I think that that's incredible," said Leslie Walker, the executive director for the Sixers Youth Foundation.

"Going from having a thousand or so people at the scrimmage to possibly 13,000? ... That's really big."

The Sixers did not keep an official attendance tally, but the arena, with a capacity of 20,478 for basketball games, appeared more than half full, and there were fans lined up in the atrium more than 10 deep an hour before tipoff, waiting to take their seats.

One fan in attendance didn't have to go through the turnstiles.

Marvel Maxey, the Sixers' star shooting guard's 4½-month-old daughter, made an appearance on the bench, wearing white noise-canceling headphones while her dad held her and sat next to James. The image invited memories of James' first child, Bronny James, sharing the bench with his dad during the past couple of seasons -- as his Los Angeles Lakers teammate.

The Sixers did not keep an official box score for the scrimmage either, but the exhibition -- that the team limited to three 10-minute periods -- featured plenty of dunks, 3s and highlight plays to give the fans a show.

"To be able to take what we've done on the practice floor, bring it to a game-floor situation around our fans ... it was a great first step in the direction we're trying to go," James said. "And it was great to hear some cheers."

The fanfare will be part of it for this Sixers team. But that's why James is in Philadelphia. He made that clear at the start of their first week together on media day.

"We have to be comfortable with being uncomfortable," he said. "That is the best way to expedite being great. You have to fall in love with doing things that are uncomfortable. And if we can do that, then we can be a great team. If we don't do that, then we'll be like, 'Oh man, that was a great team on paper, and we had a lot of great talent, and we lost in the second round.'

"I don't want to do that. I didn't leave my family to lose in the second round. I know that for sure. So, work needs to be done, and I'm ready to put the work in."

stories.headline: Is Bijan Robinson the NFL's top RB? He is when he's in primetime
stories.summary: Bijan Robinson has the most scrimmage yards per game in primetime, and he'll get a chance to keep it rolling on 'Monday Night Football' this week.
stories.body:
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- Atlanta Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski shows high school football highlights of his players to the team on Fridays. For most, the glory days of high school set a bar few could match against NFL competition.

Then there's Bijan Robinson.

To be clear, Robinson was a superstar at Salpointe Catholic High School in Tucson, Arizona. He was the Gatorade Player of the Year as a senior in 2019. But Robinson's highlights on Friday nights don't match what he has done under the lights in the NFL.

Since the 1970 NFL/AFC merger, no player has more scrimmage yards per game in primetime than Robinson (145.4 in 11 games) with a minimum of five games, per ESPN Research. Barry Sanders is second with 126.3 scrimmage yards per game in 20 contests. OJ Simpson (123 in six games) and Jonathan Taylor (121.8 in 12 games) are third and fourth, respectively.

Robinson will try to keep it rolling Monday when the Falcons (1-2) travel to New Orleans (1-2) to face the Saints (8:15 p.m. ET, ESPN).

"For me, whether it's primetime, whether it's a 1 o'clock game, they're all the same in terms of my mentality," Robinson said. "Everybody watches you on TV, and they watch you in the stands.

"I love what Kobe [Bryant] said: 'They paid to watch you, so you got to do your job on the field.'"

Robinson was remarkable against the Green Bay Packers on "Thursday Night Football" in Week 3, leading Atlanta to a 35-14 road win. He had 29 carries for 194 yards and two touchdowns, and added another 19 yards on two receptions.

"He's an elite player," Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said. "He's one of the best in the league at any position." The Falcons signed Robinson to an offseason extension that briefly made him the highest-paid running back in NFL history. Robinson, the No. 8 pick in the 2023 draft, is under contract for three years with a base salary of $66.75 million ($22.3 million per season), which could go up to $75 million. The Detroit Lions' Jahmyr Gibbs has the highest average per year at $22.5 million.

"Bro, I don't know what to say," Packers running back Kaleb Johnson said after the Week 3 game. "He deserves every penny of that."

Robinson has picked up where he left off in 2025, when he was named first-team All-Pro. He once again leads the league in yards from scrimmage (467) and is second in rushing yards (349).

Last season, he had the two longest runs of his career -- 93 yards against the Los Angeles Rams and 81 yards against the Buffalo Bills -- on "Monday Night Football." Against the Minnesota Vikings on "Sunday Night Football" in 2025, Robinson had 168 scrimmage yards. Since Robinson debuted in 2023, he has over 20 scrimmage yards per game more than any other running back in primetime. More than Derrick Henry (123.9). More than Saquon Barkley (119.5).

In his past four primetime games, Robinson is averaging 213.8 scrimmage yards. Robinson can't explain why he has excelled in primetime. He said he's not necessarily a night person, usually going to sleep around 11 p.m. "When it's time to [play], no matter what time it is, it's time to go," Robinson said. "So, the game can be played at 12 midnight, and I'm locked in, ready to go."

That same mentality is evident when Stefanski shows high school clips of Robinson.

"Our players love playing under the lights, and that takes all of us back to high school days and Friday night lights," Stefanski said. "And every Friday team meeting, I show high school highlights of one of our players.

"We've done Bijan before, so I've seen what it looked like [under] Friday night lights out there in Arizona. It was pretty special."

Even more so against the best players in the world. It's enough for recently acquired defensive tackle Gervon Dexter Sr. to put an exclamation mark on the praise. "He's the best player I've ever seen play football."

stories.headline: Bahrain GP was the worst indictment of F1's new engine regs yet
stories.summary: There was a lot to love about Sunday's race. But it will forever be overshadowed by the mess caused by the new F1 engines.
stories.body:
SEPANG, Malaysia -- The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia already had a farcical name. Formula 1's unnecessarily complicated hybrid engines ensured the race will be remembered as one of the biggest farces in the sport's recent history.

F1's current engines, which feature a near 50-50 split between internal combustion energy and electrical battery elements, are already considered the biggest mistake the sport has made in recent times. Whenever they are consigned to the scrapheap, the foremost memories will be of Sunday's two formation laps in the rain.

"LOL, look at this," was all a laughing Max Verstappen could say over the radio as his Red Bull approached a handful of cars whose engines had simply shut down. His car had already done the same at the front of the pack a couple of minutes earlier.

It was an apt use of modern day slang: Laugh out loud was all you could really do. Collectively, and due to a perfect storm of circumstances, F1's cars had all ground to a walking speed, one after the other. The first attempt at starting the race -- already delayed 40 minutes, because these F1 cars cannot race in extremely wet conditions -- was aborted, with another wait to allow the 11 teams to download and implement a software update from the governing FIA.

"Horrible," said reigning world champion Lando Norris after the race. "It just proves that we shouldn't have any of that stuff on the electronic side".

George Russell, who also dealt with a heartbreaking late engine failure which has all but handed Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli the 2026 championship, said, "The whole day was a bit of a faff. It didn't feel very F1 today".

Carlos Sainz summed up the situation best of all: "I think F1 needs to have a hard look at themselves and see how we ended up in this situation."

There's a lot to still love about F1 in 2026, and some of it was on show towards the end of Sunday's chaotic race. But the absolute worst of the sport was also showcased in brutal fashion before a competitive lap had even been completed.

What exactly happened?
As well as new-look cars and new V6 turbo hybrid engines, this year introduced a new set of Pirelli tyres. The Italian company's wet-weather tyres have been a question-mark all season, however: bar a February test behind closed doors in Spain and wet-weather tests for Red Bull, Racing Bulls and Ferrari earlier in the year, no teams had done any meaningful runs on the intermediate or full wets prior to this weekend.

The FIA immediately delayed the start as the weather intensified, with a nearby thunderstorm also complicating things. Several teams briefly lost their weather radars on the pit wall, while some of the marshal panels lining the circuit briefly stopped working.

At 3:40 p.m. local time, 40 minutes after the race was supposed to start, the FIA attempted to get things underway with two formation laps behind the safety car, followed by a standing start from the grid. The rain had started easing off and the track was wet, but it looked as though race control was going to make a go of it. But those formation laps were always going to be an exercise in extreme caution.

Several corners into the first formation lap is where things started going wrong, when the cars encountered a software bug baked into the algorithms that dictate F1's new complicated engines. During rain, for safety reasons, engine modes run at a maximum deployment of 250 kilowatts of deployment in certain sectors, down from 350kW in dry conditions. Once Verstappen, leading the pack but tiptoeing around on the cold intermediates, dropped below a speed of 50 km/h, the algorithms dictating the behaviour of his engine started having problems: essentially, the MGU-K no longer kicked in to feed power into his low-revving engine. The restriction on the car's hybrid-electric component is meant to prevent teams from effectively using it as a traction control device at the start of a race; this time, however, the combination of not running on wet tires with an extremely wet tarmac meant drivers were applying much less throttle than normal.

The algorithm did not spot the difference, so kicked in. With the additional power boost locked out, the internal combustion engine was effectively dying without a surge of recovery power from the electrical side.

You wouldn't be the only one confused by this: F1 drivers have said this year's debriefs with engineers are longer and more complicated than ever. Many have spoken about their engines behaving in radically different ways lap to lap, as self-learning algorithms kick in power at different points.

In the moment, what was happening was unclear: Some thought Verstappen simply had an engine issue.

"There was nothing going on," he said later. "That was the problem. It was just like driving at, what, 35 km/h, going uphill, actually losing speed. So, yeah, I don't know exactly, because when you go too low in speed and too low RPM, for whatever reason, then it just bogs down. Normally it takes one or two seconds and it comes back."

But this time, the power did not come back. Verstappen's car was slowing so dramatically, which meant the cars behind him bunched up. But the rules state you cannot overtake the car in front on a formation lap.

"I triggered it first and then I look in my mirror, I just see... I was like, "Wait, are they waiting for me or what's going on...?" Verstappen said.

Those behind were, in fact, waiting. The same thing happened to Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, in second position, shortly after his car also dropped below the all-important 50 km/h benchmark.

"It was like the Lego race," Hamilton joked later, referring to the viral pre-race spectacle during the Miami Grand Prix in May.

While Verstappen somehow managed to avoid coming to a complete standstill, Hamilton's ground to a halt. The seven-time world champion had to restart his Ferrari's power unit on the pit straight. But unlike with Verstappen, cars slowly started passing Hamilton as he plummeted down the order.

"It was insane," said current championship leader Antonelli. "At some point we were five-wide in the straight, because we couldn't understand what was going on."

Hamilton's Ferrari seemed to suffer the most extreme version of the engine issue: By the time he did stop completely, he was half way down the order, and Audi, Williams, Racing Bulls and other teams' cars were facing similar issues around him. It was this scene a laughing Verstappen would later drive past. The start procedure was canceled, effectively a red flag.

And here is where the lack of wet tire usage this year had caught the FIA out.

"We didn't manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked, because there's been very little wet running this year," the governing body's single seater chief Nikolas Tombazis explained in a rare trip to the media pen after the race.

"There was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in. Basically, [on] the formation lap, some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely. That bug prevented the power from being redeployed, and for the cars to start again. I think if we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time, and not have such a situation.

"Once the problem happened, our guys realised very quickly what was happening, and had to work under a lot of time pressure for an update to the software, which was issued to the teams, and the teams had to install it on their cars.

The FIA later gave a simpler statement on what had happened, blaming a perfect storm of various factors. The governing body said "an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars".

The remedy was a software update -- code Tombazis admitted was a "cobbled up, hurried solution." Rewriting and sending the new code to the teams to install in their systems led to another delay. It meant the worst of the rain also disappeared, we got only a handful of laps on the intermediates and the prospect of a genuine wet-weather classic disappeared.

If you still need another way to think about it: The 11 teams competing in the pinnacle of motorsport hit Ctrl+Alt+Delete and installed a software update to race safely again.

The fallout
The FIA did apologize afterward for the chaos.

"All of that took about 20 minutes," Tombazis said. "It may have felt like five hours for spectators waiting in a race and for everybody else, which is understandable. And we are sorry about that. But I think it was quite a fast reaction given the problem."

The sport's governing body could easily direct critics toward a race ultimately full of incidents and overtaking. And, fair enough: Sepang was an entertaining spectacle.

Verstappen returned to the top step for the first time this season. Hamilton turned in a supreme drive for third after gambling incorrectly on slick tires over intermediates, which had him over a minute down on the lead early. Antonelli now looks certain to become the sport's youngest ever champion after Russell's late DNF (and the engine penalties likely to come with it).

It was a fitting return for the brilliant Sepang circuit, too. Yet, the engines are such a step in the wrong direction it's hard to look past it.

"That's what happens when you have these engines," Verstappen said. He's been outspoken about the regs since the first time he drove a 2026 car, so it's perhaps not a surprise what he said next.

"With a V8 you don't have these problems".

F1's current rules were drawn up over a period of years, and the promise of the V6 turbo hybrid engines was making the sport more appealing to new manufacturers -- Audi this year, General Motors by the end of the decade. But the price to lure two new manufacturers to the sport does not seem worth it so far.

F1 will make small tweaks to the engines over the next two years, shifting the 50-50 split closer towards a 60-40 split in favor of conventional combustion power over the electrical elements by 2028. But many in the paddock believe it will not be enough to make racing feel normal again.

Sainz, who has been vocal about the situation, believes the sport has to learn from Sepang. "It is clear the regs are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the PUs, for the manufacturers," he said after the race. "Again, my only question mark is: Who, five years ago, decided that this was the direction to go?

"The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can with what was decided four or five years ago, but clearly what was decided four or five years ago is wrong."

A silver lining to end on: Sunday's engine farce may end up accelerating the push to drop V6s in favour of V8s at the earliest possible opportunity.

Whenever that day is, it cannot be soon enough.

stories.headline: Nigerian connection runs through Mystics rise as Kiki Iriafen breaks out in playoff run
stories.summary: Fresh from helping team USA win the World Cup last month, Kiki Iriafen's second WNBA season ended with a first round elimination to the Atlanta Dream.
stories.body:
Fresh from helping USA win the World Cup last month, Kiki Iriafen's second WNBA season ended with a first round elimination to the Atlanta Dream, but finishing the game with yet another double-double was an indication of just how quickly the Nigerian-American forward has grown into a central piece of the Washington Mystics' present.

Iriafen helped herself to 15 points and 16 rebounds in Washington's 93-75 loss to the Atlanta Dream, completing her first postseason with double-doubles in both games of the first-round series for an average of 15 points and 15 rebounds in the playoffs after a regular season in which she emerged as Washington's leading rebounder and one of their top three scorers.

Alongside her for much of that run was Michaela Onyenwere - another Nigerian-American forward whose contribution came from a different place. The 2021 WNBA Rookie of the Year came to Washington with five seasons of league experience to help the youngest roster in the WNBA and became enough of a veteran voice that her teammates began calling her "Coach Mic."

And just like she did on her Draft night when strutting it out in a dress that reflected her Nigerian heritage, Iriafen says she is driven by the Nigerian spirit

"My Nigerian heritage has been something that I've always wanted to promote," she said. "Michaela and I were just talking about what should we do. Like, we should go celebrate. But it's super special. My Nigerian heritage has been something that I've always wanted to promote. I am Nigerian American, but I feel like both sides of me are equally as important to me."

Together, both have given Washington the Nigerian connection within a team that improved from 16 wins in 2025 to a franchise-record 28 this season and returned to the playoffs for the first time since 2023.

Iriafen's rise, to go with the likes of USA teammate Sonia Citron, and Shakira Austin, was at the heart of that improvement.

After averaging 13.3 points and 8.5 rebounds as a rookie, the 23-year-old increased those numbers to 15.3 points and 9.5 rebounds this season while shooting better than 50% from the field. She finished behind Austin and Citron in scoring and led the Mystics in rebounding, narrowly ahead of Austin.

She also recorded a Mystics single-season record 23 double-doubles, and earned a second consecutive All-Star selection - numbers that helped get her onto Team USA's World Cup roster.

The postseason provided another test - one that Iriafen confronted head on, even if it was her first experience.

Foul trouble in Game 1 meant she played only 23 minutes against Atlanta, but still finished with 15 points and 14 rebounds. Nine of those rebounds came on the offensive end, tying a Washington franchise record for offensive rebounds in a game and helping the Mystics outrebound the Dream 50-31.

"I really felt like I wasn't able to help my team in the first half, so I wanted to do that for my teammates," Iriafen said.

Game 2 was much better, as she stayed on the floor for more than 35 minutes. Her 30 rebounds over the two games were the second-most by a player through her first two WNBA playoff games.

The numbers continued a progression that began almost immediately after Washington selected her with the No. 4 pick in the 2025 draft. Initially, the Mystics leaned heavily on Iriafen's rebounding, transition running and ability to finish around the basket. Now, her offensive responsibilities have gradually expanded to include more post touches, screening actions and opportunities to make decisions with the ball.

Her development has also come alongside Citron - Washington's other cornerstone from the 2025 draft. Citron led the Mystics in playoff scoring with 25 points in each game against Atlanta, while Iriafen controlled the glass.

The partnership leaves Washington with two young players who have already translated regular-season production into the postseason - one that coach Sydney Johnson was pleased with as he singled both out for praise.

"I'm sitting beside two players who played their first playoff games, and there was a lot of good stuff out there," he said. "I'm immensely disappointed for the result, but I also think what this group has accomplished and how the DC community has rallied around this group has been amazing. They've written history. I am excited to take this first step forward with Kiki and Sonia and our whole group."

For Iriafen, that development has unfolded alongside an identity she has repeatedly said matters a lot to her.

"Being Nigerian is huge for me," Iriafen told House of Victory earlier this year. "It's my culture, it's a big part of who I am.

"There are so many young Nigerian hoopers and young Nigerians that I'm an inspiration to and I just want to showcase that being Nigerian is cool."

That connection was there well before she played her first WNBA game. Who can forget Kiki owning the show at the 2025 WNBA draft in a custom dress designed by Nigerian designer Nneka Alexander, while accompanied by members of her family equally attired in traditional Nigerian clothing?

"My parents always say Naija no dey carry last," she said. "So I feel like in everything that I do, I try to strive for that. So that's kind of the motto of my life.

"Something in Nigeria is the resources aren't always as equal, but just understanding that it doesn't matter how you get there, there's still an opportunity. There's still a way. So I just really want to carry myself with class and really truly be a great role model."

The draft took her to Washington, which offered an even bigger connection to Nigeria, with its huge Nigerian population.

A year later, the Mystics added Onyenwere, whose route to the capital was considerably longer. Selected sixth overall by New York in 2021, Onyenwere won WNBA Rookie of the Year before stops with Phoenix and Chicago. Washington signed her to a multiyear deal this year and immediately installed her in a starting lineup filled with younger players.

Onyenwere, 26 years old when the season began, was the oldest player on the roster.

"We call her 'Coach Mic.' She knows what she's talking about," Iriafen said. "She's a great leader, great teammate and great person."

The connection between them predates the Mystics. They first crossed paths when Iriafen was a high school prospect considering UCLA and Onyenwere was playing for the Bruins.

Their Nigerian heritage provided another common thread. Onyenwere's father Peter competed for Nigeria in track and field, and her grandmother became one of the memorable images of the 2021 WNBA draft when she danced in traditional Nigerian clothing behind Onyenwere during a television interview when her name was called.

"I am just so proud to be Nigerian, and I never let anyone forget it," Onyenwere said. "I make sure I let people know I am Nigerian because it is a big part of who I am.

"From Draft Night, I was getting messages from young Nigerian kids who are in Nigeria, saying you are an inspiration. You don't really think those things until you see those messages. Like, I am influencing people in a different continent."

Both women have also represented the United States internationally - a clear sign of the dual identity they have carried and basked in through their basketball careers. Iriafen helped the United States win the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup, appearing in four games during the Americans' unbeaten run to the title.

Onyenwere represented USA Basketball in both 3x3 and 5-on-5 competition in 2019. She played on the American 3x3 circuit and later helped the United States win silver at the Pan American Games.

Nigeria did attempt to bring Onyenwere into the D'Tigress program for the 2024 Paris Olympics, but she was unable to join the team after failing to receive clearance in time.

In adding to the Nigerian connection, her role in Washington this season has been more about helping to provide stability around a young core.

Onyenwere averaged 9.0 points during the regular season while starting alongside Iriafen, Austin and Citron. She scored eight points in the opening playoff loss to Atlanta before adding 12 in Game 2.

Washington's season ended there, but Iriafen's first experience of playoff basketball provided another marker in a second season in which her responsibilities and production grew and both playoff games provided a clear measure of how far her role has expanded and where Washington could take it next.

She finished the two-game series averaging 15 points and 15 rebounds, with 13 offensive rebounds, after leading Washington in rebounding during the regular season and establishing career highs in both scoring and rebounding.

"This whole season has just been just a learning process for me," Iriafen said after Game 2. "It was nothing like my first season.

"I feel like just even during my undergrad, doing tough majors and still being a professional athlete, just showcasing that, whatever you put your mind to that you can do it."

For the Mystics, the next part of that learning process will be figuring out how much more Iriafen can handle. They already have one of the league's most productive young rebounders and an increasingly reliable interior scorer. Her three assists in Game 2 also offered a glimpse of how her role could expand as a passer and decision-maker.

Onyenwere, meanwhile, provided an experienced voice alongside her during that development, four years after becoming WNBA Rookie of the Year herself, giving the Mystics a Nigerian-American one-two punch.

The season may have ended earlier than they or the Mystics wanted, but it also provided a silver lining, with Washington back in the playoffs and Iriafen having experienced the stage that she wanted, even if she failed to conquer it. For now.

"Playoffs are the biggest stage," Iriafen said after Game 1. "This is the stage we want to be on."

On the evidence of this run, it is one that she will be returning to for the foreseeable future. And she will continue to be driven by that Naija no dey carry last spirit.

stories.headline: Magpies likely to hold De Goey as Pendlebury departs
stories.summary: The door has been left ajar for Collingwood to trade away Jordan De Goey as the Magpies wave goodbye to club legend Scott Pendlebury.
stories.body:
The door has been left ajar for Collingwood to trade away Jordan De Goey as the Magpies wave goodbye to club legend Scott Pendlebury.

Collingwood have been busy in the early stages of the AFL trade period, bringing in delisted GWS forward Jesse Hogan for pick No.75 in the draft after already landing dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale as a free agent.

The Magpies also traded 38-year-old Pendlebury to Gold Coast for pick No.65, with the Suns wanting to avoid diluting any free agent compensation it would yield for letting Ben King walk to Hawthorn.

With those deals locked in, Collingwood list boss Justin Leppitsch indicated a move for midfield-forward De Goey was unlikely with a year to run on his contract.

"Jordy's goals are to make sure he gets that last contract, whether that be at the Collingwood Football Club or somewhere else," Leppitsch told reporters on Monday.

"If it doesn't happen now, he'll play on next year and he may or may not finish his career with us.

"I spoke to him Friday night about it at the best and fairest ... at this point in time, we don't think anything happens."

Collingwood are yet to discuss a new contract with De Goey's camp but didn't rule out extending the 30-year-old before round one next season.

Leppitsch also expects defender Dan Houston to be at the club in 2027, declaring speculation about his future was being driven by an "external source".

A two-time All Australian, Houston has four years left on his contract after crossing from Port Adelaide in 2024 as part of a three-team mega trade.

Collingwood have had early discussions with Richmond on contracted two-time premiership player Jayden Short, but Leppitsch indicated a potential deal was a "still a bit far off".

"Jayden's probably going to be probably a little tougher," he said, citing list spots, salary expectations and Richmond's asking price.

stories.headline: UFC 332 takeaways: Talbott, Silva validate their top billing
stories.summary: Payton Talbott finished another former champion in Deiveson Figueiredo on a night full of knockouts at UFC 332.
stories.body:
The options were plenty for performance bonuses after UFC 332 in Salt Lake City. The fight card set a UFC record for knockouts with 11, and nine came in the first round. The most resounding KO went to men's bantamweight Payton Talbott in the co-main event. He came out strong, sending former champion Deiveson Figueiredo to the canvas twice before finishing him a little over two minutes into the fight. The win is Talbott's second in a row over a former champion and likely means big things ahead for him, but the loss for Figueiredo doesn't do anything to minimize his legacy in the UFC.

The main event, which received prefight chatter over whether it was worthy of a headlining slot, was high energy but mostly one-sided. Natalia Silva, the No. 1 women's flyweight contender, earned her first UFC championship with a unanimous decision over Wang Cong. The 29-year-old joins men's flyweight Joshua Van as the only UFC champions under 30.

Was the main event criticism validated?
The UFC took heat on social media for booking Silva vs. Wang in a main event on a numbered card. Silva was at the front of a long line of women's flyweight title contenders, no question, but it's fair to say Wang, unranked by ESPN and outside the top five in the UFC's own rankings, jumped the queue.

But while I'm on board with a lot of the criticism the UFC receives for its matchmaking, especially at a championship level, I understand what the fight promotion was going for in this case: The UFC was trying to set up a couple of possible storylines involving Valentina Shevchenko, who vacated the women's flyweight title to make the Silva-Wang title fight a possibility after suffering an undisclosed injury that will sideline her for "up to one year."

Why Wang? She might not have an extensive UFC résumé, but she beat Shevchenko in a kickboxing match in 2015. Their history is not unlike that of Alex Pereira and Israel Adesanya, who met twice in kickboxing, with Pereira winning both and knocking out Adesanya in one of those fights. It provided a setup for their UFC rivalry.

A Wang vs. Shevchenko angle became moot, as things turned out, because Silva was too much for the Chinese fighter to handle. Wang came in with a 10-1 MMA record, but she had zero fights against top-10 flyweights, and it showed. Silva, by contrast, came in having defeated former UFC champions (Jessica Andrade, Alexa Grasso and Rose Namajunas) in each of her past three fights.

Silva was too fast, too elusive and too precise with her punches and kicks. Wang had no answers, looked lost and couldn't get her offense going until the fifth round, when it was too late. Not to vindicate the prefight matchmaking criticism, but this sure was a lopsided and not-so-fiery bout, one that got booed by a crowd that had been treated to a UFC-record 11 knockouts on the night.

So now the 125-pound division is left with the Silva vs. Shevchenko storyline we were expecting to see before Shevchenko was injured. It will be interesting to see how Silva's speed holds up when she meets her predecessor with the belt, and how differently she'll fight when up against an opponent with a strong grappling game. Oddly, that wasn't even addressed in Silva's postfight interview in the cage. Shevchenko's name wasn't even mentioned. Now, that is a UFC decision worth questioning. -- Jeff Wagenheim

Quick thanks to Figueiredo

MMA loves to move quickly, and it's ready to move very fast with Talbott. Talbott is everything MMA could want in a prospect, and his future is very bright.

So before we all take off on the Talbott train (as we inevitably will), let's take a moment to shout out one of the most exciting flyweights of all time, Figueiredo.

Let's be honest, Figueiredo was always a borrowed bantamweight. He struggled to make 125 pounds, and most of the sport was happy to see him ditch the weight cut in 2023, but he was also undersized at 135.

It's easy to forget now, as UFC men's flyweight champion Van has taken the sport by storm -- but the flyweight division was still in a precarious position when Figueiredo made his mark in 2020. Henry Cejudo saved the division by knocking out TJ Dillashaw in 2018, but then eventually vacated a weight class the UFC seriously considered shutting down. Figueiredo picked up where Cejudo left off, saving the division with his one-punch knockout power and (frankly) villain charisma. He played the role of "bad guy" in his back-to-back fights against Joseph Benavidez in 2020, as well as his four-fight rivalry with Brandon Moreno.

It was inevitable when he moved up in weight, but for a three-year period, Figueiredo was the exact figure the flyweight division needed. The 38-year-old's career is undoubtedly coming to an end soon, but Figueiredo was not just a terrific fighter and champion in his prime, he will forever be remembered as a significant hero of flyweight MMA. -- Brett Okamoto

stories.body:
The run to the grand final by Newcastle has set prop Jacob Saifiti free to play the World Cup opener for Fiji in a huge boost to the Bati.

Saifiti was named in the Mick Potter coached 23-man squad by Fiji, leaked on social media, which will be ticked off pending eligibility and integrity clearances.

The squad the Bati have named includes several NRL stars but the presence of Saifiti will be vital in the round one clash with Cook Islands in Newcastle on October 18.

Saifiti, who played the most recent of his seven Tests for Fiji at the 2017 World Cup, was hit with a four-match ban for a high shot on Warriors winger Luke Laulilii in the 46-32 loss to the Warriors in round 26.

The Knights had the bye in the final round but the fact they played all four finals means Saifiti has now served his suspension.

The unavailability of star forwards Tui Kamikamica (illness) and Viliame Kikau (ankle) respectively has made veteran NSW prop Saifiti even more of a vital inclusion.

Dolphins utility Kurt Donoghoe, the RLPA bench player of the year, has been named and can play either lock or in the halves.

Wests Tigers flyer Sunia Turuva and co-captain Api Koroisau provide big game experience and flair.

Turuva could well play fullback due to Tigers teammate Jahream Bula missing the tournament due to post-season shoulder surgery.

The Bati have been top performers at the World Cup and reached the semi-finals in 2008, 2013 and 2017 only to be knocked out by Australia on each occasion.

stories.headline: Transfer rumors, news: Arsenal among clubs chasing winger Yildiz
stories.summary: Arsenal, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich are all chasing Juventus winger Kenan Yildiz. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
Arsenal, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich are all chasing Juventus winger Kenan Yildiz. Plus, could Endrick leave Real Madrid for AC Milan?

Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Real Madrid are pushing for Kenan Yildiz with Arsenal and Bayern Munich also looking at the Juventus winger, reports Corriere dello Sport. Juve have been demanding at least €100 million for the 21-year-old for a year, but Madrid are reigniting their interest in him with the view to a move in the summer. They would want to pit him and Vinícius Júnior against each other, while Arsenal see the Turkiye international as the answer to their lack of options on the left and Bayern have been watching him from afar since his departure.

- AC Milan are planning to make another attempt to sign Real Madrid striker Endrick after being unable to bring him in during the summer, reports La Gazzetta dello Sport. Madrid boss Jose Mourinho had initially refused to let the 20-year-old leave, but he has made just one substitute appearance this season that lasted four minutes. Milan's main competition from within Italy for the Brazil international is Roma, while Aston Villa were also unsuccessful in their efforts to bring him in last summer.

- Barcelona are willing to let Alejandro Balde leave on loan in January with Manchester United among the clubs interested in the left-back, according to TEAMtalk. The 22-year-old has fallen down the pecking order in Hansi Flick's squad and has only got onto the pitch once so far this season, playing the last 12 minutes in a 7-2 win over Racing Santander. The Spaniard's camp and intermediaries are already working hard to find a solution for him, while the Blaugrana could look to bring in a new left-back in 2027.

stories.headline: Cowboys flip script after Rio loss with key win over Texans
stories.summary: A week after everything went wrong late against the Ravens, Dallas rebounded with a winning drive Sunday.
stories.body:
HOUSTON -- One week after enduring a 10-hour flight home from Rio de Janeiro after a debilitating 34-31 loss to the Baltimore Ravens, the 45-minute flight back home from Houston on Sunday night had to feel a lot better for the Dallas Cowboys.

Questions surrounded the Cowboys following the loss to the Ravens -- especially about coach Brian Schottenheimer, defensive coordinator Christian Parker, special teams coordinator Nick Sorensen, and how the coaches managed the final 28 seconds of a game they were 2 yards away from potentially winning.

Against the Houston Texans (0-4) on Sunday, the Cowboys were trailing 30-27 with 2:25 left, facing a 1-3 start to the season for the second straight year.

But quarterback Dak Prescott and receiver CeeDee Lamb helped lessen the temperature around the coaches and players by connecting on a 12-yard touchdown with 40 seconds to go for a 34-30 must-have victory.

"Rio doesn't define us as a football team, as a coaching staff here," Schottenheimer said. "I think I was very upfront and honest with that, but I wanted this game. Why? Because these guys came back off a 10-hour trip. The Ravens, I think, played at home today. We played on the road. We play Thursday night [against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers].

"We'll play anybody anywhere and we're looking forward to that, but Rio had nothing to do with this game. This game stood by itself."

But the fate of a season might have been on the line with a loss. Since 2000, the Cowboys have never opened a season with one victory in the first month of the season and finished above .500. The best they have done is last year's 7-9-1 in Schottenheimer's first season.

In the first half, a Cowboys' offense that wants to be considered "The Greatest Offense There Is" failed to score a touchdown. In the second half, they scored touchdowns on their first three possessions, then Prescott delivered with the late winning drive.

In certain moments, the defense was better. Linebacker Rashan Gary had his first sack in 12 games, dating to last season with the Green Bay Packers. Defensive end Quinnen Williams had his first sack of the season, dropping C.J. Stroud for an 11-yard loss in the fourth quarter. In the first three games, the Cowboys had two sacks. They had three Sunday.

But the unit still gave up eight pass plays of at least 20 yards.

Schottenheimer wasn't concerned about his decision at the end of the half when he opted to have Brandon Aubrey attempt a 65-yard field goal despite the Texans being out of timeouts. When Aubrey's kick hooked a little left, the Texans were able to convert a field goal of their own to take a 16-6 halftime lead.

"We felt very comfortable that Brandon would make that kick," Schottenheimer said. "And at that point in the game, I had no question that if for some reason he missed it, that we had plenty of time to fight back."

He was proved correct as Prescott directed the winning 11-play, 74-yard drive that ended with Lamb (17 catches, 189 yards) in the end zone with 40 seconds left. Along the way, the Cowboys also needed to convert a fourth-down play.

Before the game, Prescott acknowledged to thinking what a 1-3 start would have meant.

"That can't happen," he said. "During the game, I'm the most optimistic guy there is."

Seven days earlier inside Maracanã Stadium, Prescott had the Cowboys in position to beat the Ravens, but then just about everything went wrong.

On Sunday, things went right. Prescott credited Schottenheimer's playcall for the Lamb touchdown. The kickoff ran time off the clock. The defense was able to keep everything in front of them, and Stroud's Hail Mary attempt throw fell incomplete.

For only the third time in Prescott's 10-plus seasons as the starter, the Cowboys overcame a double-digit deficit to win a game. Before Sunday, they had lost 32 straight road games when trailing by double digits in the second half, which was the longest active streak in the league.

"There's nothing like winning," Prescott said. "I want to say it fixes all the problems, but it doesn't. It makes you feel good at least for a day or so. But at this point, we got to turn the page and get ready for Thursday. We can't sit here and have some winning hangover. It's so early in the season.

"It's no different than last week's loss. ... Just shows the resilience of this team to win. So now it's about stacking these wins with great momentum and just belief in the team that we've created."

stories.headline: Max Verstappen praises Red Bull on 'very special' Bahrain Grand Prix win after 'tough start to year'
stories.summary: Max Verstappen praised Red Bull's resilience through a tough start to 2026 after he delivered the team an "amazing" first win with its own engine at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen praised Red Bull's resilience through a tough start to 2026 after he delivered the team an "amazing" first win with its own engine at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Verstappen turned in a spectacular drive at Sepang, recovering from a poor start from pole position to pass Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli on route to his 72nd career win with Red Bull.

It was the team's first under the new V6 turbo hybrid regulations, which saw it stop buying engines from other manufacturers and build and compete with its own, built at its UK headquarters in Milton Keynes.

Verstappen said it felt like a landmark moment for the project.

"Of course, very special for us," Verstappen said after Sunday's race, which featured a rain delay, a farcical aborted start and then a chaotic race in changing conditions.

"I mean, we had a very complicated and tough start to the year with all sorts of problems and just not being competitive enough. But throughout the year, the team has been working very hard to understand our issues and bring good performance upgrades to the car and make it more driveable. Step by step, we've been getting closer and closer, and today, and of course especially this whole weekend, we've been really in good form. So, yeah, it's amazing.

"Very, very enjoyable to win here and also have our first victory for our own engine. I mean, it's an incredible project with a lot of partners and a lot of people that are dedicated to be where we are now. So, yeah, [a] fantastic feeling."

- Max Verstappen wins disrupted Bahrain GP, Kimi Antonelli extends title lead as George Russell retires

- Bahrain GP in Malaysia: George Russell suffers major title blow after race retirement

- Lewis Hamilton: No plans to visit casino with Ferrari strategists after slick tyre gamble

TV footage showed Verstappen's father Jos looking emotional after the victory during the podium ceremony.

Verstappen only just committed to a new Red Bull contract last month, but had delayed that decision as he pondered whether he wanted to stay in the sport.

The four-time world champion said his father and those close to him know how difficult this season has been behind the scenes.

"We're all very much invested in it," Verstappen said. "And, of course, you know, my relationship with my dad, we really understand each other well from all the years that we have spent together working towards our goal in Formula 1. So he's still there in the background. He's not coming every race, but when he is there, we talk a lot about everything. He knows everything.

"And, yeah, also for him, I guess the beginning of the season was not nice to watch, as for me being in the car was not nice to drive. But then seeing how the team progressed and basically never really stopped working and really took the car and just really tried to fix the issues that we had, and then deliver something like this, it's amazing. And also with the people involved, honestly, the spirit in the team is very good. Everyone is on the same line and we really understand each other well. So it's very enjoyable to work in the team and that's why I think also everyone is super happy that we finally delivered a result like this."

Verstappen's victory means he now has won a race in each of the last 10 seasons -- only the two drivers ahead of him on the all-time winners' list, Michael Schumacher and Lewis Hamilton, have done the same.

stories.headline: Lacob lauds Williams as world's best after Valkyries' Game 1 win
stories.summary: Gabby Williams scored 25 points and played lockdown defense in a performance that led Valkyries owner Joe Lacob to declare her the "best player in the world."
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Golden State Valkyries owner Joe Lacob walked through the tunnels of Chase Center following the Valkyries' 71-60 win over the Las Vegas Aces in Game 1 of the WNBA semifinals with a message he wanted to get off of his chest.

"Print this: Gabby Williams is the best player in the world," Lacob told ESPN.

Williams scored a team-high 25 points Sunday afternoon and scored or assisted on 36 of the Valkyries' points. On the other end, she held the Aces to just 29% on 4-of-14 shooting as the primary defender. Williams, who also had 11 rebounds and five assists, became the second player with 25 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a playoff game against the Aces. She is also the first Valkyries player to have a 25-10-5 playoff game.

After arriving in Golden State during the offseason, Williams has taken her play to another level with the Valkyries -- finishing second in Defensive Player of the Year voting and also adding to her offensive game. So far, she's averaging 25 points during the playoffs, which is the third-highest scoring average of the postseason. Only Wilson and Arike Ogunbowale have scored more.

Early in the game Sunday, Williams felt that the Aces were trying to make her uncomfortable, throwing a mixture of coverages at her. That's when she made sure she was intentional about getting everyone else involved.

"There are five players on the court," Williams said. "We were running really well in transition, so I found [Kayla Thornton] a couple times, and things started to open up on their own."

The Valkyries' ability to get out and run was fueled by their performance on the boards. Golden State outrebounded Las Vegas 52-25 -- the second-largest difference by any team in a playoff game in WNBA history. It also held the Aces to a season low in scoring.

The Aces made pushes, clawing back from down by as much as 11, but they never took away Golden State's momentum and couldn't get their deficit below five points down the stretch of the game.

"All we talked about the last 48 hours was rebounding and blocking them out, and we did not do that. Period," Aces coach Becky Hammon said. "The good news is, we played like ass and only lost by 10."

A'ja Wilson finished with 24 points on 8-of-21 field goal shooting and went 8-of-11 from the free throw line. Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young combined for 25 points.

"I've competed against A'ja my entire career, and she will go down in history as the best player to ever do it," Williams said. "This is what you dream about. You dream to play against players like that. Going up against them is all I care about. ... I just want to win."

Williams rolled her eyes when she heard what Lacob said about her, but the belief he has poured into her is the reason she is leading the Valkyries in their playoff push. During every game, she seeks out a fist bump from the owner to "absorb" some of his energy. When she watches replays of the game, she zooms in to see his spirited reaction to big plays.

"There she is," Lacob yelled when he saw Williams standing in the hallway after the game, his arms open for a hug. "Best player in the world. No one is saying it, but they need to start saying it."

stories.headline: Merrett moves to Hawks as Bombers avoid ugly trade war
stories.summary: Zach Merrett can breath a sigh of relief, with the former Essendon captain headed to Hawthorn after the bitter AFL rivals agreed to a trade.
stories.body:
Zach Merrett can breath a sigh of relief, with the former Essendon captain headed to Hawthorn after the bitter AFL rivals agreed to a trade.

Hawthorn and Essendon locked in a deal for the 31-year-old on Monday afternoon, hours after the AFL trade window opened.

The Hawks will give up picks No.15 and No.25 in this year's draft, plus a 2028 second-round pick, in exchange for the seven-time Bombers best and fairest and three-time All Australian.

The midfielder joins Hawthorn on a long-term contract, reportedly worth $4 million over four years with a trigger for a fifth season.

"Zach has long been celebrated as one of the most elite midfielders in the AFL, and he will play a key role in our side for many years to come," Hawthorn list boss Mark McKenzie said.

"His professionalism and competitiveness are second to none."

In 2025, Essendon knocked back Hawthorn's final offer of two first-round picks (10 and 22), a future first-rounder, and now-delisted midfielder Henry Hustwaite.

Bombers president Andrew Welsh had warned Hawthorn not to get "too cute with us again" in an interview with the Herald Sun.

McKenzie said the Hawks had learned after waiting until about 30 hours before the 2025 trade deadline to make first contact with Essendon about Merrett.

Merrett, who was entering the final year of his contract, stepped down as Essendon captain but featured in all 23 matches on his way to securing a seventh Crichton Medal.

Essendon paid tribute to the 274-gamer as the defining Bomber of his generation.

"When people look back on this era of Essendon, Zach's name will be one of the first they mention," Essendon chief executive Tim Roberts said.

With the Merrett deal done, Hawthorn's attention will turn to acquiring Gold Coast key forward Ben King as a restricted free agent.

The Hawks are expected to lodge paperwork for King on Tuesday, with the Suns afforded three days to match their contract offer.

Gold Coast list boss Kall Burns said the Suns would take their time to consider whether to match or accept band one compensation, currently valued at pick No.7.

"You've got to weigh up what you can possibly get in if it's a trade," he said.

"It is only day one of the trade period."

Hawthorn fell at the preliminary final hurdle for a second straight year, losing to eventual premiers Brisbane by nine points.

stories.headline: USMNT's young stars shine to give Pochettino 'fantastic problem'
stories.summary: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino said that the number of players performing at a high level is "a fantastic problem to have" after teenagers Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall propelled the USMNT to 3-0 win over rivals Mexico on Saturday.
stories.body:
GLENDALE, Ariz. -- United States men's national team coach Mauricio Pochettino said that the number of players performing at a high level is "a fantastic problem to have" after teenagers Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall propelled the USMNT to 3-0 win over rivals Mexico on Saturday.

The U.S. endured a difficult first half, and scored completely against the run of play in the 28th minute when Hall converted from close range after Mexico keeper Raúl Rangel spilled Gio Reyna's low cross right in front of goal.

- Cavan Sullivan has arrived: U.S. phenom's goal caps a memorable win over Mexico

- Márquez bemoans 'terrible mistakes' as Mexico humbled by USMNT

- USMNT player ratings: Sullivan, Hall 9/10 in big win vs. Mexico

The USMNT began to make more headway in the second half, and doubled its lead in the 62nd minute when Sullivan intercepted a pass from Rangel, and chipped the ball into the net from 35 yards out. The match lost its edge when Mexico's Mateo Chávez was red carded in the 67th minute following a scrap with Sebastian Berhalter.

Malik Tillman finished off the scoring in the 84th minute, latching onto another wayward Mexico pass to firing into the net.

Hall, 18, is just the third USMNT player to score in his first three national team appearances, while 17-year-old Sullivan became the youngest scorer in USMNT history.

"I think it's a fantastic problem for us," Pochettino said about the performances of his team's young players. "I think we will take the right decision in the right moment, but I think it's a very good problem to see.

"Now it's not a moment at all, but yes, we appreciate that situation and of course hope that we will be in that situation that young players perform in the way that they deserve to be with us."

Pochettino also pronounced himself pleased with the way his side weathered Mexico's early pressure.

"I think that this, overall, was a great opportunity to discover ourself, to see ourselves in a difficult game with a very good team. Again, Mexico is a great team," Pochettino said.

"Yes, I think two different maybe halves. The first half I think Mexico started really well. They forced us to play back. We never connected. We were losing all the duels. And then we start to grow after 15, 20 minutes. And I think it was a good lesson the first half because it was the sense of work all together, suffer together even when you are not playing well in the way that you plan to play."

But Pochettino couldn't help but admire the performance of Sullivan, who impressed with his work on both sides the ball.

"I think he's a talented player with enormous quality, but with a very good balance, in possession and out of possession," Pochettino said about Sullivan. "He's a fighter, he's a warrior. It's difficult to find this type of player with a tremendous quality.

"And then I think Cavan showed in possession with the ball on the field [and] when he need to be chasing people and recover the ball. That is my impression after maybe three weeks together. And that is unbelievable, to have a player like this. I think it's a fantastic news for USA. Hope that continues in that way."

Pochettino was careful to laud Sullivan's young teammates as well, who have largely impressed during this window.

"It's a big moment because we need to be right with them," Pochettino said about the win, and the path forward. "We need to protect them. We need to support them. Our responsibility now is that this group of talented players grow in the right direction."
